title: Binding Parameters Safely
learning_outcomes: Describe the main purpose and behavior of binding parameters safely.
Apply a small SQLite example involving positional parameters and verify the result.
Identify one failure mode, compatibility constraint, or data-integrity concern related to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson covers binding parameters safely as part of SQLite’s embedded relational database model. Work through one small example, verify the output, and then connect the result to the listed subtopics from the supplied curriculum.
content.why_it_matters: Parameters represent values, while dynamic identifiers require allow-lists.
content.task: Create a second example for binding parameters safely. Use at least one of these subtopics: Positional parameters, Named parameters, Binding values by type. Predict the result, run it in a local SQLite environment or supported language binding, and document one boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Include a minimal reproducible SQL statement or application snippet.
State the expected result before execution and compare it to the observed result.
Document one boundary/error case and the SQLite runtime assumptions.
hints: Start from the smallest subtopic and a fixture with only a few known rows.
Write the expected output before running the example; then change one input or predicate and compare.
If a feature fails, verify the linked SQLite version/build and isolate the failing statement before changing the schema.

common_mistakes.why: SQLite has specific type-affinity, NULL, configuration and version behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Check SQLite’s official documentation and the actual linked runtime; reduce to a small fixture.

common_mistakes.why: A query can run successfully while returning incorrect rows or an inflated aggregate.
common_mistakes.fix: Compare output to a hand-calculated expected result and test an edge case.

common_mistakes.why: Destructive SQL and migration experiments can permanently change a database.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable file or in-memory database and verify backups before destructive operations.

summary: Bind untrusted values as parameters; do not concatenate input into SQL syntax.
Record SELECT sqlite_version() and the relevant feature/build assumptions.
Keep a reproducible example and expected output so later changes can be regression-tested.
content.run_instructions: Save as `sqlite_demo.py` and run with Python 3.10+ (`python sqlite_demo.py`). This illustrates the standard library sqlite3 binding; confirm the application’s linked SQLite version with `sqlite3.sqlite_version`.
content.troubleshooting: Use one placeholder per value and pass values as a tuple. Do not interpolate untrusted text into SQL. Check the Python sqlite3 module’s linked runtime, not just the standalone CLI.
content.reset_steps: Close the shell and delete only the disposable `practice.db` file, or use a fresh `:memory:` connection. Never reset a production database.

items.title: Positional parameters
items.text: Keep SQL syntax separate from user-supplied values using bound parameters. Parameters cannot stand for table/column names; dynamic identifiers should come from a strict allow-list.

content_blocks.title: Example: Binding Parameters Safely
content_blocks.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL)')
con.execute('INSERT INTO notes(title) VALUES (?)', ('First note',))
row = con.execute('SELECT title FROM notes WHERE id = ?', (1,)).fetchone()
print(row[0])
con.close()

items.title: Assuming generic SQL behavior
items.text: Check SQLite’s own documentation and the actual linked runtime; standards-compliant engines can still differ in type handling, SQL extensions, and configuration.

content_blocks.text: Recap. Bind untrusted values as parameters; do not concatenate input into SQL syntax. Keep the binding parameters safely behavior explicit in code and document assumptions that a future maintainer would otherwise have to guess.
